facts.statement: The genus Xenacanthus was first described by Beyrich in 1848.
Pleuracanthus is a synonym for the genus Xenacanthus.
Xenacanthus is an extinct genus of xenacanthid shark named after its distinctive spine.
facts.quote: Xenacanthus (from Ancient Greek ξένος, xénos, 'foreign, alien' + ἄκανθος, akanthos, 'spine') is an extinct genus of xenacanthid shark.

facts.statement: Xenacanthus lived in freshwater environments and its fossils have been found worldwide.
facts.quote: It lived in freshwater environments, and fossils of various species have been found worldwide.

facts.statement: Xenacanthus decheni grew to about 1 meter, while X. meisenheimensis reached up to 1.2 meters.
facts.quote: X. decheni reached about 1 m, X. meisenheimensis reached up to 1.2 m, X. (Expleuracanthus) gaudryi reached 58 cm.

facts.statement: Xenacanthus parallelus was one of the smallest species, with fully grown males reaching 20 cm and females 34 cm.
facts.quote: X. parallelus is one of the smallest xenacanths, males reached 20 cm and females reached 34 cm, both are fully grown.

facts.statement: Xenacanthus had a ribbonlike dorsal fin that ran the entire length of its back and joined the anal fin at the tail.
facts.quote: The dorsal fin was ribbonlike and ran the entire length of the back and round the tail, where it joined with the anal fin.

facts.statement: Xenacanthus likely swam in a manner similar to modern conger eels due to its fin arrangement.
facts.quote: This arrangement resembles that of modern conger eels, and Xenacanthus probably swam in a similar manner.

facts.statement: Researchers speculate that the distinctive spine of Xenacanthus may have been venomous, similar to a sting ray.
facts.quote: The spike has even been speculated to have been venomous, perhaps in a similar manner to a sting ray.

facts.statement: Xenacanthus fossils are known from the Carboniferous-Permian periods in North America, Europe, and South America.
facts.quote: Fossils are known from the Carboniferous-Permian of North America, Europe, and South America.

facts.statement: Isotopic measurements indicate Xenacanthus was a euryoecious genus inhabiting rivers, oligotrophic lakes, and eutrophic lakes.
facts.quote: Paired δ18OP and 87Sr/86Sr measurements of the teeth of Xenacanthus indicate that it was a euryoecious genus, inhabiting rivers in addition to oligotrophic and to eutrophic lakes.

facts.statement: Xenacanthus lived from the Pennsylvanian to the Permian, until about 280 million years ago.
facts.quote: Xenacanthus es un género extinto de tiburones que vivieron entre el Pensilvánico, en el Pérmico, hasta hace 280 millones de años.

facts.statement: Xenacanthus had a thin, elongated body with a dorsal fin extending from the head to the tip of its triangular tail.
facts.quote: Su cuerpo era fino y alargado, con una aleta dorsal que iba desde la cabeza hasta la punta de su triangular cola.

facts.statement: A spine ran along the entire body of Xenacanthus, from the skull to the tip of the tail.
facts.quote: Una espina recorría todo su cuerpo, desde el cráneo hasta la punta de la cola.

facts.statement: The spine of Xenacanthus was not associated with fish cartilage but likely had tissue covering it so they appeared like vertebrae.
facts.quote: Esta espina no se asocia con el cartílago de los peces ya que posiblemente tenía algún tipo de tejido que las recubría de forma que parecían vértebras.

facts.statement: The spine-like structures of Xenacanthus allowed its fossils to be preserved in better condition than those of other sharks because bone preserves better than cartilage.
facts.quote: Esta característica ha permitido que los fósiles se conserven en mejor estado que los de otros tiburones, ya que el hueso se conserva mejor que el cartílago.

facts.statement: Xenacanthus lived in New Mexico, United States.
Xenacanthus belongs to the class Chondrichthyes, subclass Elasmobranchii, order Xenacanthiformes, and family Xenacanthidae.
facts.quote: regnum: Animalia phylum: Chordata classis: Chondrichthyes subclassis: Elasmobranchii ordo: Xenacanthiformes familia: Xenacanthidae

facts.statement: The time range for Xenacanthus is from the Moscovian to the Norian, between 312.8 and 205.7 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Moscovian to Norian (312.8 to 205.7 million years ago)
